claim: Human to mosquito transmission was assessed using 171 direct mosquito feeding assays conducted in Burkina Faso and Kenya.
source: Human to mosquito transmission was assessed using 171 direct mosquito feeding assays conducted in Burkina Faso and Kenya.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and location of feeding assays conducted.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum infects Anopheles gambiae at 4% mosquitoes at 1 gametocyte per µl blood.
source: Plasmodium falciparum infects Anopheles gambiae efficiently at low densities (4% mosquitoes at 1/µl blood), although substantially more (>200/µl) are required to increase infection further.
evidence: This is a direct result from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Substantially more than 200 gametocytes per µl are required to increase mosquito infection further beyond the level achieved at 1 gametocyte per µl.
source: Plasmodium falciparum infects Anopheles gambiae efficiently at low densities (4% mosquitoes at 1/µl blood), although substantially more (>200/µl) are required to increase infection further.
evidence: This finding is derived from the analysis of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.

claim: In Burkina Faso, children harbour more gametocytes than adults.
source: In a site in Burkina Faso, children harbour more gametocytes than adults though the non-linear relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection means that (per person) they only contribute slightly more to transmission.
evidence: This is based on cross-sectional survey data from Burkina Faso.

claim: Due to the non-linear relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection, children only contribute slightly more to transmission per person than adults despite having more gametocytes.
source: In a site in Burkina Faso, children harbour more gametocytes than adults though the non-linear relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection means that (per person) they only contribute slightly more to transmission.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from combining gametocyte density data with the transmission model.

claim: Interventions reducing gametocyte density need to be highly effective in order to halt human–mosquito transmission.
source: Interventions reducing gametocyte density need to be highly effective in order to halt human–mosquito transmission, although their use can be optimised by targeting those contributing the most to transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the non-linear relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.

claim: Male and female gametocytes are ingested by the mosquito and reproduce sexually in its stomach before developing into oocysts.
source: Male and female transmission stages (gametocytes) are ingested by the mosquito and reproduce sexually in its stomach before developing into oocysts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the malaria parasite life cycle.

claim: Once oocysts establish, it is assumed that mosquitoes will form infectious sporozoites.
source: Once oocysts establish, it is assumed that mosquitoes will form infectious sporozoites, so the proportion of mosquitoes developing oocysts is used as a measure of mosquito infectivity.
evidence: This is a stated assumption in the manuscript based on established knowledge.

claim: The proportion of mosquitoes developing oocysts is used as a measure of mosquito infectivity.
source: Once oocysts establish, it is assumed that mosquitoes will form infectious sporozoites, so the proportion of mosquitoes developing oocysts is used as a measure of mosquito infectivity.
evidence: This is the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: In Plasmodium falciparum, mosquito infection is thought to increase with the number of gametocytes ingested by the mosquito.
source: In the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, mosquito infection is thought to increase with the number of gametocytes ingested by the mosquito (Jeffery and Eyles, 1955; Graves et al., 1988; Bousema and Drakeley, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Several studies have failed to find an association between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.
source: However, several studies have failed to find an association (Boudin et al., 1993; Haji et al., 1996), and the precise shape of the relationship has never been rigorously quantified, particularly at very low gametocyte densities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The precise shape of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection has never been rigorously quantified, particularly at very low gametocyte densities.
source: However, several studies have failed to find an association (Boudin et al., 1993; Haji et al., 1996), and the precise shape of the relationship has never been rigorously quantified, particularly at very low gametocyte densities.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this study.

claim: Microscopy may miss up to 80% of parasites.
source: Difficulties arise because estimates of gametocyte density have relied on microscopy, which may miss up to 80% of parasites (Dowling and Shute, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Pfs25mRNA quantitative nucleic acid sequence–based amplification (QT-NASBA) is a more sensitive molecular method than microscopy for detecting gametocytes.
source: More sensitive molecular methods such as Pfs25mRNA quantitative nucleic acid sequence–based amplification (QT-NASBA) have been developed (Schneider et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: QT-NASBA enables gametocyte densities to be quantified over the entire epidemiologically relevant range.
source: Unlike conventional microscopy, this technique enables gametocyte densities to be quantified over the entire epidemiologically relevant range.
evidence: This is a stated advantage of the QT-NASBA technique.

claim: Transmission reduction is now a key component of global efforts to control and eliminate malaria.
source: Transmission reduction is now a key component of global efforts to control and eliminate malaria (Alonso et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A wide range of novel transmission-reducing drugs and vaccines are currently under development.
source: A wide range of novel transmission-reducing drugs and vaccines are currently under development, which aim to reduce malaria incidence by restricting human to mosquito transmission.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of malaria intervention development.

claim: The transmission-reducing ability of artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) is gaining increased attention.
source: The transmission-reducing ability of front-line therapeutics (such as artemisinin-based combination therapies [ACTs], or potential combinations of ACTs with gametocytocidal drugs) is also gaining increased attention (WHO, 2012; White, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to WHO and other research.

claim: Mathematical models of malaria transmission tend not to include explicitly the relationship between gametocytaemia and mosquito infectivity.
source: Mathematical models of malaria transmission tend not to include explicitly the relationship between gametocytaemia and mosquito infectivity, opting, for simplicity, to assume density-independent transmission probabilities (Smith et al., 2007; Griffin et al., 2010), or fit functions to the relationship between the number of asexual parasites and the probability of a blood-feeding mosquito becoming infected (Ross et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Greater complexity in mathematical models will be required to capture fully malaria population dynamics following the introduction of drugs and vaccines that specifically target transmission stages.
source: Greater complexity, however, will be required to capture fully malaria population dynamics following the introduction of drugs and vaccines that specifically target transmission stages.
evidence: This is an inference about the needs for future modeling work.

claim: WHO has recommended that in pre-elimination or elimination malaria programmes, single-dose primaquine (0·25 mg base per kg) with an ACT should be given to all patients with falciparum malaria except pregnant women and infants <1 year old.
source: For example, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recently recommended that in pre-elimination or elimination malaria programmes, single-dose primaquine (0·25 mg base per kg) with an ACT should be given to all patients with falciparum malaria except pregnant women and infants <1 year old (WHO, 2012).
evidence: This is a WHO recommendation cited in the manuscript.

claim: The human reservoir of infection is likely to vary between different endemic settings.
source: The optimal use of transmission-reducing interventions will also require a better understanding of the human reservoir of infection, which is likely to vary between different endemic settings.
evidence: This is a statement about expected variation in epidemiological patterns.

claim: Various studies have attempted to estimate the relative contribution of different age groups to mosquito infection using skin or membrane feeding assays.
source: Various studies have attempted to estimate the relative contribution of different age groups to mosquito infection using skin or membrane feeding assays (Muirhead-Thomson, 1957; Graves et al., 1988; Boudin et al., 1991; Githeko et al., 1992; Drakeley et al., 2000; Bonnet et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Mosquito feeding assay studies are logistically complicated and expensive.
source: These studies are logistically complicated and expensive, so more efficient methods of determining the reservoir of infection are required in order to target interventions optimally.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of conducting feeding assays.

claim: The relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection is highly non-linear.
source: The relationship between the number of gametocytes in the blood and mosquito infection was found to be highly non-linear (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the data analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum infects mosquitoes at very low gametocyte densities that predominate in natural infections and may not be detected using standard microscopy.
source: Plasmodium falciparum infects mosquitoes at the very low gametocyte densities that predominate in natural infections and may not be detected using standard microscopy (Bousema and Drakeley, 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by citation.

claim: Infection rises rapidly with increasing gametocyte density up to 1 gametocyte per microlitre.
source: Infection rises rapidly with increasing gametocyte density, and by 1 gametocyte per microlitre, ∼4% (95% Bayesian credible interval [CI], 3–5%) of all mosquitoes develop oocysts.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The Gompertz model gave the best fit to the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection with a DIC of 1034.
source: The subsequent increase in infection with increasing gametocyte density is best described by the Gompertz model (deviance information criterion [DIC] = 1034), which gave a significantly better fit than the linear (DIC = 1073), power (DIC = 1059), or hyperbolic (DIC = 1062) functions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model comparison.

claim: The Gompertz model gave a significantly better fit than the linear, power, or hyperbolic functions.
source: The subsequent increase in infection with increasing gametocyte density is best described by the Gompertz model (deviance information criterion [DIC] = 1034), which gave a significantly better fit than the linear (DIC = 1073), power (DIC = 1059), or hyperbolic (DIC = 1062) functions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from model comparison using DIC values.

claim: The best-fit model predicts that increasing density from 1 to 200 gametocytes per microlitre does not appreciably increase infection.
source: The best-fit model predicts that increasing density from 1 to 200 gametocytes per microlitre does not appreciably increase infection.
evidence: This is a prediction from the fitted Gompertz model.

claim: Beyond 200 gametocytes per microlitre, infection rises again to finally plateau at approximately 18% infected mosquitoes.
source: Beyond 200 gametocytes per microlitre, infection rises again to finally plateau at ∼18% infected mosquitoes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the fitted model.

claim: Gametocyte density on an arithmetic scale was a better predictor of mosquito infection than gametocyte density on a logarithmic scale.
source: Gametocyte density on an arithmetic scale was a better predictor of mosquito infection than gametocyte density on a logarithmic scale.
evidence: This is a result from comparing different model formulations.

claim: Including information on the host's asexual parasite density significantly improved model fit.
source: Including information on the host's asexual parasite density significantly improved model fit.
evidence: This is a statistical result from model comparison.

claim: Children with asexual parasite densities between 1 and 1000 parasites per microlitre were on average 27% (CI, 19–58%) less infectious to mosquitoes than those with no detectable asexual parasites.
source: Children with asexual parasite densities between 1 and 1000 parasites per microlitre were on average 27% (CI, 19–58%) less infectious to mosquitoes than those with no detectable asexual parasites, whereas those with asexual densities >1000 µl−1 were 77% (CI, 14–140%) more infectious.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the regression analysis.

claim: Children with asexual densities >1000 µl−1 were 77% (CI, 14–140%) more infectious to mosquitoes than those with no detectable asexual parasites.
source: Children with asexual parasite densities between 1 and 1000 parasites per microlitre were on average 27% (CI, 19–58%) less infectious to mosquitoes than those with no detectable asexual parasites, whereas those with asexual densities >1000 µl−1 were 77% (CI, 14–140%) more infectious.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the regression analysis.

claim: Including age improves the fit of the model suggesting that age is an important confounder.
source: Including age improves the fit of the model suggesting that age is an important confounder, although the Bayesian credible intervals include 0.
evidence: This is a result from model comparison and statistical analysis.

claim: Children >6 years old were 15% (CI, 24–64%) more likely to infect mosquitoes than those of younger ages.
source: Children >6 years old were 15% (CI, 24–64%) more likely to infect mosquitoes than those of younger ages, whereas no difference in the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection was detected between Burkina Faso and Kenya.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the regression analysis, though the credible interval includes negative values.

claim: No difference in the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection was detected between Burkina Faso and Kenya.
source: Children >6 years old were 15% (CI, 24–64%) more likely to infect mosquitoes than those of younger ages, whereas no difference in the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection was detected between Burkina Faso and Kenya.
evidence: This is a result from comparing the two study sites in the analysis.

claim: Reducing gametocyte density by 99% in a host with 200 gametocytes per microlitre may not have much effect on their immediate contribution to transmission.
source: For example, reducing gametocyte density by 99% in a host with 200 gametocytes per microlitre may not have much effect on their immediate contribution to transmission (Figure 1B), although it will probably reduce the duration of infectivity.
evidence: This is an inference from the non-linear relationship shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Reducing gametocyte density by 99% in a host with 200 gametocytes per microlitre will probably reduce the duration of infectivity.
source: For example, reducing gametocyte density by 99% in a host with 200 gametocytes per microlitre may not have much effect on their immediate contribution to transmission (Figure 1B), although it will probably reduce the duration of infectivity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the temporal effects of intervention.

claim: The same intervention efficacy at reducing gametocyte density in a host with 300 gametocytes per microlitre would cause an appreciable reduction in human to mosquito transmission from that individual.
source: The same intervention efficacy at reducing gametocyte density in a host with 300 gametocytes per microlitre would cause an appreciable reduction in human to mosquito transmission from that individual.
evidence: This is an inference from the non-linear relationship between gametocyte density and transmission.

claim: In the cross-sectional survey in Burkina Faso, 10 year olds have five times as many gametocytes compared to 50 year olds.
source: In the cross-sectional survey in Burkina Faso, children harbour more gametocytes than adults, with 10 year olds having five times as many gametocytes compared to the 50 year olds (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cross-sectional survey data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Adults in Burkina Faso are only 37% less likely to infect mosquitoes compared to children, infecting on average 3.5% of them.
source: However, the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection established here means that adults are only 37% less likely to infect mosquitoes (infecting on average 3.5% of them, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from applying the transmission model to the age-stratified gametocyte data.

claim: At the time of the survey conducted in Burkina Faso, the peak in the reservoir of infection occurs at an earlier age than the peak in gametocyte density.
source: Results indicate that, at the time of the survey conducted in Burkina Faso, the peak in the reservoir of infection occurs at an earlier age than the peak in gametocyte density, which will improve the (cost) effectiveness of school-based programmes.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the age profiles of gametocyte density and transmission potential.

claim: The earlier peak in the reservoir of infection compared to gametocyte density will improve the cost-effectiveness of school-based programmes.
source: Results indicate that, at the time of the survey conducted in Burkina Faso, the peak in the reservoir of infection occurs at an earlier age than the peak in gametocyte density, which will improve the (cost) effectiveness of school-based programmes.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications for intervention targeting.

claim: If an intervention can keep gametocyte density beneath 200 gametocytes per microlitre in a low transmission area, it may be sufficient to push the basic reproduction number of malaria beneath one and eliminate the disease.
source: If an intervention can keep gametocyte density beneath 200 gametocytes per microlitre in a low transmission area, it may be sufficient to push the basic reproduction number of malaria beneath one and eliminate the disease.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings for elimination.

claim: The distribution of gametocytes between hosts is highly overdispersed and adequately described by the negative binomial distribution.
source: However, the highly overdispersed distribution of gametocytes between hosts (adequately described by the negative binomial distribution) means that in the population from Burkina Faso, 30% of transmission comes from hosts with densities beneath the microscopy detection threshold of 16 gametocytes per microlitre.
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the distribution of gametocytes in the population.

claim: In the population from Burkina Faso, 30% of transmission comes from hosts with densities beneath the microscopy detection threshold of 16 gametocytes per microlitre.
source: However, the highly overdispersed distribution of gametocytes between hosts (adequately described by the negative binomial distribution) means that in the population from Burkina Faso, 30% of transmission comes from hosts with densities beneath the microscopy detection threshold of 16 gametocytes per microlitre.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from applying the model to the Burkina Faso population data.

claim: Evaluating interventions solely on their ability to reduce microscopically detectable gametocytes may give misleading results.
source: This means that evaluating interventions solely on their ability to reduce microscopically detectable gametocytes, as has been suggested (Graves et al., 2012), may give misleading results.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that substantial transmission comes from submicroscopic infections.

claim: It is unclear whether asexual parasites directly influence parasite infectivity or are associated with other unmeasured variables such as the multiplicity of infection or factors influencing the blood environment such as immunity.
source: It is unclear whether asexual parasites directly influence parasite infectivity or are associated with other (here unmeasured) variables such as the multiplicity of infection (Nsango et al., 2012) or factors influencing the blood environment such as immunity (Bousema and Drakeley, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the mechanism underlying the observed association.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum has asynchronous waves of asexual and sexual parasites.
source: Plasmodium falciparum has asynchronous waves of asexual and sexual parasites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. falciparum biology.

claim: Circulating gametocytes take 2–3 days to mature before they can infect mosquitoes.
source: Circulating gametocytes take 2–3 days to mature before they can infect mosquitoes (Lensen et al., 1999), which may explain the complicated relationship between infectivity and asexual density (i.e., intermediate asexual parasite densities might occur at the start of gametocyte production and have a relatively low proportion of infectious mature gametocytes).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Intermediate asexual parasite densities might occur at the start of gametocyte production and have a relatively low proportion of infectious mature gametocytes.
source: Circulating gametocytes take 2–3 days to mature before they can infect mosquitoes (Lensen et al., 1999), which may explain the complicated relationship between infectivity and asexual density (i.e., intermediate asexual parasite densities might occur at the start of gametocyte production and have a relatively low proportion of infectious mature gametocytes).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed relationship between asexual density and infectivity.

claim: On average, older children were more infectious, supporting previous indications that transmission-reducing immunity may predominate in young children.
source: On average, older children were more infectious, supporting previous indications that transmission-reducing immunity may predominate in young children (Drakeley et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Individual QT-NASBA gametocyte density estimates are relatively uncertain.
source: Figure 1A indicates that individual QT-NASBA gametocyte density estimates are relatively uncertain.
evidence: This is an observation about the measurement error visible in Figure 1A.

claim: QT-NASBA gametocyte density estimates are considerably more accurate than conventional microscopy.
source: Despite this, they are considerably more accurate than conventional microscopy.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about diagnostic methods.

claim: Measures of precision such as confidence intervals or standard errors around gametocyte density estimates are rarely reported in the scientific literature.
source: Even though uncertainty is generally accepted by those conducting the experiments, measures of precision such as confidence intervals or standard errors around such density estimates are rarely reported in the scientific literature.
evidence: This is an observation about reporting practices in the field.

claim: It has been suggested that the marker used in this analysis (Pfs25 mRNA) might be parasite female specific.
source: Care should be taken when interpreting gametocyte density estimates as it has been suggested that the marker used in this analysis (Pfs25 mRNA) might be parasite female specific (Schneider, 2006).
evidence: This is a caveat about the QT-NASBA method supported by citation.

claim: If the current QT-NASBA method does only detect female gametocytes, it will neither change the qualitative conclusions of this study nor their application if other studies use the same technique.
source: Even if the current QT-NASBA method does only detect female gametocytes, it will neither change the qualitative conclusions of this study nor their application if other studies use the same technique.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the conclusions.

claim: Direct comparison of results with those of studies using different methods for quantifying gametocyte density should be aware that the shape of the relationship may differ.
source: However, direct comparison of our results with those of studies using different methods for quantifying gametocyte density should be aware that the shape of the relationship may differ.
evidence: This is a caveat about comparing results across different methodologies.

claim: Gametocyte density measurement error is likely to cause the majority of the uncertainty seen in model outputs.
source: Gametocyte density measurement error is likely to cause the majority of the uncertainty seen in model outputs, although the complexity of the membrane feeding assay is also likely to contribute.
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of uncertainty in the analysis.

claim: The complexity of the membrane feeding assay is likely to contribute to uncertainty in model outputs.
source: Gametocyte density measurement error is likely to cause the majority of the uncertainty seen in model outputs, although the complexity of the membrane feeding assay is also likely to contribute.
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of uncertainty in the analysis.

claim: The proportion of mosquitoes infected by Plasmodium-infected blood is known to vary substantially within and between studies.
source: The proportion of mosquitoes infected by Plasmodium-infected blood is known to vary substantially within and between studies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about variability in feeding assay results.

claim: Variability in mosquito infection rates is in part due to methodological issues with the membrane feeding assay.
source: This is in part due to methodological issues with the membrane feeding assay (Bousema et al., 2013) but also related to biological differences in the parasite-vector combination and the blood environment (Bousema and Drakeley, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Variability in mosquito infection rates is related to biological differences in the parasite-vector combination and the blood environment.
source: This is in part due to methodological issues with the membrane feeding assay (Bousema et al., 2013) but also related to biological differences in the parasite-vector combination and the blood environment (Bousema and Drakeley, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Further standardising the membrane feeding assay would improve the accuracy of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.
source: Further standardising the membrane feeding assay, improving the accuracy of QT-NASBA technique and the inclusion of additional covariates (such as estimates of gametocyte maturity, which have been investigated in Plasmodium vivax; Chansamut et al., 2012), would improve the accuracy of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Improving the accuracy of QT-NASBA technique would improve the accuracy of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.
source: Further standardising the membrane feeding assay, improving the accuracy of QT-NASBA technique and the inclusion of additional covariates (such as estimates of gametocyte maturity, which have been investigated in Plasmodium vivax; Chansamut et al., 2012), would improve the accuracy of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Including additional covariates such as estimates of gametocyte maturity would improve the accuracy of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.
source: Further standardising the membrane feeding assay, improving the accuracy of QT-NASBA technique and the inclusion of additional covariates (such as estimates of gametocyte maturity, which have been investigated in Plasmodium vivax; Chansamut et al., 2012), would improve the accuracy of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research supported by citation to work in P. vivax.

claim: Care should be taken when interpreting the results of feeding assays as the mosquitoes used and their biting behaviour is likely to be different from that seen in wild mosquitoes in field situations.
source: Care should also be taken when interpreting the results of feeding assays as the mosquitoes used, and their biting behaviour is likely to be different from that seen in wild mosquitoes in field situations (Bousema et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a caveat about the generalizability of feeding assay results, supported by citation.

claim: Transmission reduction will become increasingly important as areas approach local elimination.
source: Transmission reduction will become increasingly important as areas approach local elimination.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of transmission reduction in elimination contexts.

claim: In the high transmission site in Burkina Faso, young children harbour the majority of gametocytes but are only slightly more infective to mosquitoes than adults.
source: In the high transmission site in Burkina Faso, young children harbour the majority of gametocytes but are only slightly more infective to mosquitoes than adults.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the Burkina Faso cross-sectional survey analysis.

claim: The per person contribution of adults to transmission estimated in this study is considerably greater than that predicted by other mathematical models.
source: The per person contribution of adults estimated here is considerably greater than that predicted by other mathematical models (Ross et al., 2006) and may increase further once age-dependent biting rates are taken into consideration (Carnevale et al., 1978; Ross et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous modeling work supported by citations.

claim: The per person contribution of adults to transmission may increase further once age-dependent biting rates are taken into consideration.
source: The per person contribution of adults estimated here is considerably greater than that predicted by other mathematical models (Ross et al., 2006) and may increase further once age-dependent biting rates are taken into consideration (Carnevale et al., 1978; Ross et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about factors not included in the current analysis, supported by citations.

claim: The contribution of different age groups to overall transmission will depend on local demography, age-dependent protection by malaria interventions, and human to mosquito contact patterns.
source: The contribution of different age groups to overall transmission will depend on local demography, age-dependent protection by malaria interventions (such as the use of bed nets or time spent in the house and therefore personally protected by indoor residual spraying), and human to mosquito contact patterns.
evidence: This is a statement about factors that influence the reservoir of infection.

claim: Human to mosquito contact patterns are difficult to measure and poorly understood, reducing our ability to accurately predict the sources of infection.
source: The last two of these are difficult to measure and poorly understood, reducing our ability to accurately predict the sources of infection.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in current knowledge.

claim: The reservoir of infection is likely to vary between endemicity settings and over time.
source: The reservoir of infection is likely to vary between endemicity settings and over time so multiple cross-sectional surveys may be required.
evidence: This is an inference about expected variation in epidemiological patterns.

claim: Multiple cross-sectional surveys may be required to characterize the reservoir of infection.
source: The reservoir of infection is likely to vary between endemicity settings and over time so multiple cross-sectional surveys may be required.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on expected variation.

claim: The relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection will allow estimates of the reservoir of infection from cross-sectional gametocytaemia surveys without the need for logistically complicated mosquito feeding assays.
source: The relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection will allow estimates of the reservoir of infection from cross-sectional gametocytaemia surveys without the need for logistically complicated mosquito feeding assays.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical application of the study findings.

claim: The results of this article should be included within mathematical models that capture changes in gametocyte density with time to evaluate the full impact that different transmission-reducing interventions will have on transmission.
source: The results of this article should be included within mathematical models that capture changes in gametocyte density with time (Lawpoolsri et al., 2009) to evaluate the full impact that different transmission-reducing interventions will have on transmission and prioritise the most appropriate candidates according to transmission setting.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future modeling work supported by citation.

claim: Given the ability of very low P. falciparum gametocyte densities to establish infection in A. gambiae, transmission-reducing interventions will need to be highly efficacious at reducing gametocyte density in order to halt human to mosquito transmission.
source: It shows that, given the ability of very low P. falciparum gametocyte densities to establish infection in A. gambiae, transmission-reducing interventions will need to be highly efficacious at reducing gametocyte density in order to halt human to mosquito transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about low-density transmission.

claim: The complex and non-linear shape of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection may explain why the ability of interventions to reduce the proportion of infected mosquitoes has been shown to depend on the parasite load of the host.
source: The complex and non-linear shape of the relationship between gametocyte density and mosquito infection may explain why the ability of an interventions to reduce the proportion of infected mosquitoes has been shown to depend on the parasite load of the host (Churcher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous observations, supported by citation.

claim: Gametocyte density changes with host age.
source: Gametocyte density also changes with host age so the effectiveness of transmission-reducing interventions that target gametocytes will also vary with age.
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-sectional survey data.

claim: The effectiveness of transmission-reducing interventions that target gametocytes will vary with age.
source: Gametocyte density also changes with host age so the effectiveness of transmission-reducing interventions that target gametocytes will also vary with age.
evidence: This is an inference from the age-dependent gametocyte density patterns.

claim: Age-dependent effectiveness of transmission-reducing interventions should be considered in clinical trials of transmission-reducing candidate drugs and vaccines.
source: This should be considered in clinical trials of transmission-reducing candidate drugs and vaccines.
evidence: This is a recommendation for clinical trial design.

claim: The highly overdispersed distribution of gametocytes in the host population and the non-linear relationship between gametocytes/asexual parasite density and mosquito infection means that the impact of different transmission-reducing interventions on overall transmission at the population level will be far from intuitive.
source: The highly overdispersed distribution of gametocytes in the host population and the non-linear relationship between gametocytes/asexual parasite density and mosquito infection means that the impact of different transmission-reducing interventions on overall transmission at the population level will be far from intuitive.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the complexity of predicting intervention impacts.

claim: QT-NASBA measures time to positivity (TTP), which is the time it takes for the number of target amplicons detected to exceed a defined threshold.
source: The assay measures time to positivity (TTP), which is the time it takes for the number of target amplicons detected to exceed a defined threshold (Schneider et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of the QT-NASBA method supported by citation.

claim: The relationship between TTP and gametocyte density is estimated by fitting a linear regression to TTP estimates generated using a sample with known gametocyte density.
source: The relationship between TTP and gametocyte density is estimated by fitting a linear regression to TTP estimates generated using a sample with known gametocyte density (a 10-fold dilution series of in vitro cultured gametocytes ranging from 106 to 101 gametocytes per millilitre).
evidence: This is a description of the calibration method used.

claim: Data from 171 mosquito feeds on patients' blood conducted in Burkina Faso and Kenya were combined to fit a quantitative relationship between gametocyte density, asexual parasite density, host age, and mosquito infection.
